newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo JAT plans to restructure, privatise by 2000.
newsitem.headline: Yugo JAT plans to restructure, privatise by 2000.

text.p: Yugoslavia's flag carrier Jugoslovenski aerotransport (JAT) said on Tuesday it planned to restructure and privatise parts of the new holding company by the year 2000 in an attempt to boost efficiency and profit.

"JAT sees itself transforming into a holding (company) with flying services acting as an umbrella company with technical maintenance, commercial division, catering and other services acting as dependent companies," JAT general manager Zika Petrovic told Reuters in an interview.
"We want to create a profitable company by 2000. But we do not intend to wait so long to begin with changes. We plan to start (restructuring) by the end of this year," he added.

JAT would retain 100-percent ownership of the operating companies. But once the restructuring is concluded all parts would be on the market, Petrovic said and added that future partners would probably be able to acquire even 100 percent stake in those accompanying services.
"We shall do this very carefully. Any restructuring and privatisation will be conducted under a special government programme on privatising big state companies," Petrovic said.
JAT has been valued at $303 million dollars, but Deloitte&Touche is working on a new estimate which is expected to be higher.
Petrovic suggested JAT could separate its technical support division and allow foreign partners to invest and use it as part of their own technical maintenance operations.
He also expected that JAT's five-star hotel Slavija, located in central Belgrade, would become a part of an international hotel chain.

Belgrade Airport, not facing the usual congestions, noise, slot and development problems, was offering some relief at Europe's periphery with complete technical support to service any type of aircraft, including jumbo-jets and even concorde, he said.
"Belgrade airport can serve Far East carriers to end their European journey, while JAT could carry their passengers on to European destinations," Petrovic said.
The airport in the Yugoslav capital was expected to qualify for the category 2 of airports -- closed for only a few days a year during winter.
Petrovic said privatisation will bring JAT fresh capital, better performance and higher quality services.

"We want to link to other companies and have an idea of a Balkan cooperation to rationalise operations. We want flying, commercial, technical, marketing, training cooperation. But we also fly to Europe and must connect with stronger and technologically more powerful companies," he said.
Petrovic said JAT, founded on April 1, 1947, already had good business ties with KLM Air France, British Airways and Alitalia.

Cooperation was vital if JAT wanted to find its place on a European market of liberalised and deregulated air services seen posing economic problems to smaller air-carriers, he said. -- Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 222 4254
